title: The University’s principles of open publishing updated
content:
The University’s principles of open publishing have been updated on 1 September 2026.

In late 2025, the University of Helsinki and other Finnish universities jointly adopted a prior licence model for research publications. Under this model, authors may openly self-archive their refereed article manuscripts simultaneously with publication. This takes place in their organisation’s publication repository under a Creative Commons licence.  

The updated University principles of open publishing take into account the changes brought about by the introduction of the prior licence model.

title: KUPOLI 20 vuotta
content:
The Research Group for the Sociology and Politics of Education, KUPOLI, was established 20 years ago by Professor (now Emeritus) Hannu Simola. Over the past two decades, KUPOLI has produced a remarkable number of articles, books, doctoral dissertations, and research projects, while also preparing a research community of several dozen scholars for a wide range of expert positions and different stages of academic careers.

Around 30 current and former members of KUPOLI gathered on 5 June 2026 to celebrate the anniversary. In his celebratory speech, Professor Janne Varjo described the essence of KUPOLI as follows:

Although people have come and gone – and sometimes come back – something fundamental has remained unchanged. Perhaps this has something to do with our shared interest in the structures of education systems and the possibilities for action they contain? Perhaps it is about the relationship between universalism and particularism, or between equality and freedom of choice? It is something that, in Jenny Ozga’s words, is ‘deeply rooted in the social science tradition, historically informed and drawing on qualitative and illuminative techniques.’

title: New course: Principles of High-Throughput Plant Phenotyping
content:
This course provides a practical and research-oriented introduction to modern high-throughput plant phenotyping. Students learn how digital imaging, sensor technologies, robotics and data analytics are used to measure plant traits efficiently across controlled and field environments. The course combines online teaching with an intensive in-person training week at NMBU and UiO.

When: 22 September – 9 October 2026
Where: NMBU, UiO and online
Credits: 5 ECTS (BIO412)

  • Core principles of plant phenotyping and biological imaging
  • Introduction to field phenotyping
  • Controlled-environment phenotyping using advanced imaging systems
  • High-throughput seed phenotyping and trait-based sorting for model and crop species
  • Image processing, machine learning and data-analysis pipelines
  • Designing phenotyping experiments and handling large datasets

    • PhD students in plant sciences, biology, biotechnology, environmental sciences or related fields. MSc students may be admitted if space allows.

    Online sessions (20 h total):

  • 22 September, 13:00–17:00
  • 25 September, 12:00–16:00
  • 29 September, 13:00–17:00
  • 2 October, 12:00–16:00

    • In-person week (5–9 October, approx. 40 h):

  • 2 days at NMBU
  • 2 days at UiO
  • 1 day for student presentations

title: Online Lecture Series 2026: Hospicing Education? Reflexive and Critical Approaches to Education and Research
content:
Inspired by ongoing conversations around hospicing modernity, the series creates space for critical and reflexive inquiry into assumptions that shape contemporary education and educational research. Across seven online lectures, researchers and scholars engage with questions related to education development, modernity, educational reform, remote teaching and educational equity, competition, participatory research, decolonial approaches and climate justice.

All lectures are held online.

title: Kotona asuvien muistisairaiden määrä voi kaksinkertaistua vuoteen 2040 mennessä
content:
The study provides the first projection based on national registry data, separately assessing the number of people with dementia living at home and in long-term care by 2040. According to the forecast, the total number of people with dementia will increase from roughly 124,000 in 2018 to approximately 216,000 by 2040 as a result of an ageing population and increased life expectancy. 

“The phenomenon is positive as such, as it indicates that more and more people are living longer. At the same time, the number of people living with dementia is growing, increasing the need for care and services,” says researcher Maria Guzman-Castillo of the University of Helsinki.

The study examined two alternative trends in the provision of institutional and residential services. 

If service provision remains at the 2018 level, the total number of long-term care clients would increase by roughly 60% to about 117,000 people by 2040. Roughly three-quarters of them would have dementia, with an estimated 126,000 people living at home with such a condition.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

content:
Date: 16th September 2026

Time: 13:00

Title: From Discovery to Impact: The Journey of Scientific Innovation

Location: Walter seminar room, Viikki EE building, Agnes Sjöbergin katu 2

Host: Paula Elomaa

Abstract: Scientific discoveries generate societal and economic impact only when they can be transformed into scalable technologies, viable products, and sustainable businesses. This presentation explores the pathway from scientific breakthrough to commercialization, highlighting the role of applied research organizations in bridging the gap between fundamental research and industrial implementation. The innovation journey is illustrated through examples from VTT and the emerging field of cellular agriculture.

title: NutriLOC launches to advance locally driven solutions for child malnutrition in Africa
content:
The new international research and innovation project NutriLOC officially was launched 1 September 2026, bringing together African and European experts and stakeholders committed to transforming the prevention and treatment of child malnutrition through locally driven, sustainable and evidence-based solutions. 

Funded through the European Union’s Horizon Europe Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, the project has a budget of EUR 4 million over the next four years. NutriLOC is coordinated by the University of Helsinki and the project consortium will convene for its official kick-off meeting on 2–3 October 2026 in Accra, Ghana.

Malnutrition in children under five remains one of the world’s most urgent and persistent global health challenges and represents a direct violation of children’s rights. Despite decades of international efforts, coverage for the treatment of severe acute malnutrition remains critically low, often reaching fewer than 20% of affected children. At the same time, moderate acute malnutrition, which affects even larger numbers of children and frequently precedes severe acute malnutrition, continues to receive insufficient attention.
